briefs.hearing:
Hearing Loss and Chronic Ear Disease

start with the Weber and Rinne tests, then read the drum: otosclerosis, cholesteatoma and the sensorineural causesWhere does the Weber go, is the drum intact, and is there a mass on it?

DiagnosisPracticeManagement
Bottom line

The tuning forks sort every hearing loss into conductive or sensorineural; they screen, and audiometry confirms. Then the drum names the conductive cause.

  • Conductive loss: Weber lateralizes to the affected ear, and Rinne shows bone conduction greater than air conduction in that ear.
  • Sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL): Weber lateralizes away from the affected ear, and air conduction stays greater than bone conduction in both ears.
  • Otosclerosis: a conductive loss with a normal otoscopic exam in a young adult.
  • Cholesteatoma: painless otorrhea that fails antibiotics and a conductive loss, from a pearly white mass in a retraction pocket behind an intact drum; treated by surgical excision.
  • Chronic suppurative otitis media: persistent otorrhea over 2 to 6 weeks through a perforated drum; discharge with an intact drum is not otitis media, and a perforation does not exclude a cholesteatoma.
  • Sensorineural mimics: presbycusis, Ménière disease, vestibular schwannoma, aminoglycosides; all have normal otoscopy.
Diagnosis
Otosclerosis Lesion – abnormal bone remodeling of the otic capsule, often starting at the fissula ante fenestram; an otospongiotic (hypervascular, resorptive) phase, then a sclerotic phase that fixes the stapes footplate · Who – autosomal dominant with about 40% penetrance, so family history is often absent; twice as common in women, suggesting a role for sex hormones; hearing loss often begins in the 20s or 30s; pregnancy appears to exacerbate it · Paracusis of Willis – hears conversation better in noisy surroundings · Schwartze sign – a reddish blush through the drum from hypervascularity in the active phase · Carhart notch – a dip in bone conduction at 2000 Hz, an artifact of ossicular fixation · Measles virus – its RNA (ribonucleic acid) has been found in otosclerotic foci · van der Hoeve syndrome – osteogenesis imperfecta, a type I collagen disorder, with otosclerosis and blue sclerae
Cholesteatoma Lesion – a benign growth of keratinizing squamous epithelium with keratin debris in the middle ear: skin in the wrong place, not a tumor and not an infection; most cases are acquired and unilateral · Acquired – chronic middle-ear disease pulls a retraction pocket into the attic; it traps epithelium, keratin accumulates, and the mass erodes toward the ossicles; it arises from pars flaccida or posterosuperior retraction · Secondary acquired – follows drum injury, usually infection or trauma, so a perforation does not exclude it · Congenital – a white mass behind an intact drum in a child with no history of ear disease, classically anterosuperior, though surgical series find it variable · Risk factors – recurrent acute otitis media, chronic effusion and tympanostomy tubes; cleft palate multiplies all three through eustachian tube dysfunction · Tested on – chronic otorrhea when the debris becomes infected, and conductive loss once it reaches the ossicles
Hearing loss and ear drainage: the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe tell
CholesteatomaRetraction pocket traps keratin, expanding toward the ossiclesPearly white mass behind an intact drum, painless refractory otorrhea

Practice
  1. 35-year-old woman has 2 years of worsening hearing in her left ear Hears conversation better in noisy places Weber lateralizes to the left ear Rinne: bone over air conduction on the left tympanic membranes normal Afebrile · BP 118/74 mm Hg → Otosclerosis → a conductive loss (Weber to the affected ear, bone over air there) with a normal drum in a young adult is otosclerosis: the stapes footplate is fixed. Hearing better in noisy places is paracusis of Willis. A sensorineural loss sends the Weber away, and a cholesteatoma shows a mass or retraction pocket on the drum
  2. 35-year-old woman has 3 months of reduced hearing in her right ear No ear pain, drainage or vertigo Weber lateralizes to the left ear Rinne: air over bone conduction in both ears tympanic membranes normal Afebrile · BP 116/72 mm Hg → Sensorineural hearing loss → the Weber goes away from the affected ear and air stays louder than bone on both sides, so the loss is sensorineural. A conductive loss, otosclerosis included, sends the Weber to the affected ear with bone over air there, though otosclerosis may add a sensorineural loss when it involves the cochlea. The forks screen; audiometry confirms
  3. 5-year-old boy has a month of purulent right ear drainage Unimproved by topical, then oral antibiotics; painless Cleft palate; prior effusions and ear tubes intact, immobile tympanic membrane superior retraction pocket with a pearly white mass conductive hearing loss Afebrile → Cholesteatoma → painless drainage that fails antibiotics, through an intact drum, from a pearly white mass in a retraction pocket, with a conductive loss: trapped squamous epithelium and keratin debris. Otitis media with discharge needs a perforation, and otitis externa is a tender canal that responds to drops. Cleft palate, effusions and tubes are its risk factors
  4. 50-year-old man has had right-sided hearing loss for 2 days It developed over a few hours; ear feels full canals clear; tympanic membranes normal Weber lateralizes to the left; air over bone conduction bilaterally Afebrile · BP 128/80 mm Hg → Sudden sensorineural hearing loss → a sensorineural loss over hours is sudden sensorineural hearing loss: audiometry as soon as possible, within 14 days of symptom onset, confirms it, MRI or auditory brainstem response looks for retrocochlear disease, and corticosteroids may be offered within 2 weeks of onset; no routine head CT or labs. Cerumen would show in the canal, and otosclerosis is a slow conductive loss
  5. 5-year-old boy was diagnosed with a right middle-ear cholesteatoma last week Drainage quieted on drops; definitive management now planned white keratin mass in an attic retraction pocket conductive hearing loss on the right Afebrile · CT: attic wall erosion → Surgical excision → surgical excision is the treatment; antibiotics control the infected debris but do not remove the epithelium or stop the destruction. Tympanostomy tubes treat effusions, not a keratin mass
  6. 45-year-old woman has 8 months of worsening hearing in her left ear Constant ringing in that ear; mild unsteadiness walking No spinning vertigo Weber lateralizes to the right; air over bone conduction bilaterally Afebrile · BP 122/78 mm Hg → Vestibular schwannoma → unilateral sensorineural loss with tinnitus is a vestibular schwannoma until MRI with gadolinium of the internal auditory canals shows otherwise; head CT can miss a small one. Ménière disease brings episodic vertigo with fluctuating loss, and presbycusis is gradual, bilateral and high-frequency
  7. 3-year-old girl has had 2 days of fever and left ear pain This morning pus drained from the ear, and the pain eased bulging, red tympanic membrane noted yesterday today purulent fluid in the canal T 38.6 °C · HR 128/min → Oral antibiotic therapy → pain and fever, then sudden drainage with relief, is acute otitis media with perforation: the infection under pressure ruptured the drum. A child 6 months or older with otorrhea gets antibiotic therapy for 10 days, high-dose oral amoxicillin first, so drops alone fall short; excision is for a cholesteatoma, which drains painlessly
  8. 68-year-old man has had trouble following conversations for several years No vertigo; no loud-sound exposure at work or leisure audiogram: symmetric high-frequency sensorineural loss poor speech discrimination tympanic membranes normal BP 134/82 mm Hg → Presbycusis → gradual, bilateral, high-frequency loss in an older adult, with poor understanding of speech, is presbycusis; hearing aids are the mainstay. Ménière disease brings episodic vertigo with fluctuating loss and tinnitus, and loud-sound injury needs the exposure and typically starts at 4 kHz
  9. 12-year-old girl on a swim team has 3 days of right ear pain pain on pulling the tragus swollen, red, macerated ear canal tympanic membrane normal Afebrile · no facial weakness → Topical antibiotic drops → tragal tenderness with a macerated canal and a normal drum in a swimmer is otitis externa; topical drops are first line, and oral antibiotics are for cellulitis beyond the canal, immunocompromise, diabetes, or when drops cannot be used. Computed tomography is for the necrotizing form, with granulation tissue and cranial neuropathies. Water is a canal risk; the drum sorts the risk lists
  10. 2-year-old boy has bilateral hearing loss found last month Passed newborn hearing screen; no family history of deafness Petechiae and low birth weight at birth; no newborn antibiotics small head, circumference below the 3rd percentile audiogram: bilateral sensorineural loss Afebrile → Congenital cytomegalovirus infection → petechiae, low birth weight and a small head are signs of congenital cytomegalovirus infection at birth, and its hearing loss can be present at birth or develop later and may progress with age, so a passed newborn screen does not exclude it. A connexin 26 mutation is the commonest hereditary cause, but it is autosomal recessive, so parents usually hear normally and family history is often absent; it does not cause petechiae or a small head. Aminoglycosides need a drug exposure, and this child had no newborn antibiotics
  11. 9-year-old girl was diagnosed with a left middle-ear cholesteatoma 2 months ago Awaiting surgery; since yesterday cannot close her left eye new left facial droop, forehead included foul drainage from the left ear Afebrile · BP 104/66 mm Hg → Urgent imaging and surgical referral → a new facial palsy on the side of a known cholesteatoma is facial nerve erosion, which converts an elective operation into an urgent one: imaging and surgical referral now. Bell palsy is a diagnosis of exclusion, and otologic disease such as a cholesteatoma should not be overlooked; watching with audiometry leaves the erosion running
  12. 3-year-old girl has bilateral hearing loss found at a preschool screening Older brother has worn hearing aids since infancy Development otherwise normal; no newborn intensive care audiogram: bilateral sensorineural loss tympanic membranes normal Afebrile → Connexin 26 mutation → an affected sibling points to a hereditary cause, and a connexin 26 mutation is the commonest cause of hereditary sensorineural loss. Congenital cytomegalovirus is the commonest nonhereditary cause, and aminoglycosides need a drug exposure
  13. 68-year-old man with diabetes has 3 weeks of severe left ear pain granulation tissue at the bony-cartilaginous junction of the canal new left facial nerve palsy T 37.8 °C · glucose 280 mg/dL → Computed tomography with intravenous antipseudomonal therapy → severe pain, granulation tissue at the bony-cartilaginous junction and a cranial neuropathy in a diabetic patient is necrotizing otitis externa: computed tomography with intravenous antipseudomonal therapy. Drops treat uncomplicated canal disease, and excision treats a cholesteatoma
  14. 35-year-old woman has 4 months of foul-smelling right ear drainage Painless; antibiotic drops give only brief relief posterosuperior retraction pocket filled with white debris pars tensa intact Weber lateralizes to the right; bone over air conduction there Afebrile → Cholesteatoma → a conductive loss with foul, painless drainage from a retraction pocket is cholesteatoma, typically posterosuperior. Persistent drainage over 2 to 6 weeks through a perforation is chronic suppurative otitis media, though a perforation would not exclude a cholesteatoma; this drum is intact; serous otitis media is fluid behind an intact drum, and middle-ear fluid drains only through a perforation
  15. 8-year-old boy was diagnosed with a right cholesteatoma 1 month ago Now brief spinning vertigo when his right ear canal is pressed nystagmus on pneumatic otoscopy of the right ear conductive loss on the right Afebrile · HR 90/min → Urgent surgical referral → vertigo on canal pressure is a labyrinthine fistula: erosion into the inner ear, which converts an elective operation into an urgent one. A vestibular suppressant hides it, and Epley repositioning treats posterior canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, brief spells brought on by head position
  16. 2-year-old boy has bilateral hearing loss found when his speech lagged No family history of hearing loss No ear infections; no loud sound exposure audiogram: bilateral sensorineural loss tympanic membranes normal, no effusion Afebrile → Congenital cytomegalovirus infection → with no family history, no exposure and no syndrome, the commonest nonhereditary cause of sensorineural hearing loss in children is congenital cytomegalovirus infection, often asymptomatic at birth, with hearing loss that may be delayed. An effusion gives a conductive loss with an abnormal drum, and loud-sound injury needs the exposure
  17. 4-year-old boy has reduced right-ear hearing found at a school screening No past ear infections, effusions or ear tubes round white mass behind an intact drum, anterosuperior quadrant Weber lateralizes to the right; bone over air conduction there Afebrile → Congenital cholesteatoma → a white mass behind an intact drum in a child with no history of ear disease is congenital, and needs no retraction pocket to explain it. Acquired disease arises from pars flaccida or posterosuperior retraction after middle-ear disease, and tympanosclerosis is chalky white patches in the drum after otitis or tubes
  18. 10-year-old girl has 6 months of painless, foul left ear drainage white debris in a posterosuperior retraction pocket Weber lateralizes to the left; bone over air conduction there tympanic membrane otherwise intact Afebrile · temporal bone CT: ossicular erosion → The expanding keratin mass erodes and immobilizes the ossicular chain → the expanding keratin mass erodes and immobilizes the ossicles, so sound never reaches an intact cochlea: a conductive loss. Nerve compression at the internal auditory canal and endolymphatic hydrops are sensorineural
  19. 5-year-old boy was diagnosed with a left cholesteatoma after a month of drainage Malodorous drainage persists on drops pearly white mass in an attic retraction pocket conductive loss on the left Afebrile → Another course of topical and oral antibiotics → another antibiotic course treats the superinfection rather than the lesion: it may quiet the drainage, but it does not stop the destructive process. Surgical excision, through an otolaryngology referral, is the treatment
Management
Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (2019 otolaryngology guideline) Distinguish sensorineural from conductive loss at the first visit, and look for bilateral loss, recurrent episodes and focal neurologic findings. Obtain audiometry as soon as possible (within 14 days of symptom onset) to confirm it, and MRI or auditory brainstem response (ABR) for retrocochlear disease; no routine head CT and no routine labs. Corticosteroids may be offered as initial therapy within 2 weeks of onset; intratympanic steroids should be offered for incomplete recovery 2 to 6 weeks after onset; hyperbaric oxygen combined with steroids may be offered within 2 weeks of onset, or within 1 month as salvage. Antivirals, thrombolytics, vasodilators and vasoactive substances are not routine. Repeat audiometry at the end of treatment and within 6 months of completion.
Cholesteatoma Treated primarily by surgical excision. Topical and oral antibiotics may quiet the superinfected debris and slow growth, but they do not stop the destructive process, so another course will not resolve it. Erosion into neighboring structures, facial nerve palsy, a labyrinthine fistula with vertigo on canal pressure, or, rarely, intracranial complications, converts an elective operation into an urgent one; the absence of vertigo argues against a fistula.
By diagnosis Otosclerosis: hearing aids, or stapedectomy or stapedotomy with a prosthesis. Presbycusis: hearing aids are the mainstay. Chronic suppurative otitis media: topical quinolones, equally or more effective than aminoglycosides and without their ototoxicity risk. Otitis externa: topical drops; oral antibiotics only for cellulitis beyond the canal, immunocompromise, diabetes, or when drops cannot be used. Necrotizing otitis externa: computed tomography with intravenous antipseudomonal therapy.
Canal and middle-ear risk factors Canal: water exposure, trauma from swabs or ear candling, foreign material such as hearing aids and headphones, and skin conditions such as eczema. Water strips antibacterial cerumen, raises the canal pH, macerates the skin and introduces organisms; Pseudomonas aeruginosa grows in water. Middle ear, not canal: sick contacts, incomplete immunization, tobacco smoke, prior tympanostomy tubes and recurrent acute otitis media. The drum separates the two, so a middle-ear risk factor transfers no risk to the canal.
Pearls Middle-ear infection drains only through a perforation, so otorrhea with an intact drum comes from the drum itself or the canal. Purulent drainage over a month is the cholesteatoma's debris becoming superinfected, which is why antibiotics give only partial, temporary responses. A conductive loss that appears after normal audiometry is new: something in the ear has changed. A conductive loss localizes to the ossicles, so a cholesteatoma causing hearing loss is already eroding them. Immobility on insufflation means the drum is tethered by the pocket.
Common wrong answers Acute otitis media with an inflamed drum for painless drainage: it needs a bulging or inflamed drum, and drainage implies a perforation. Foreign body: the mass is in the drum, not the canal, with no removal attempts. Otitis externa: topical therapy failed, and a discrete mass on the drum is not a canal finding. Schwannoma: sensorineural loss with tinnitus in adulthood, NF2 stigmata in a child. Head CT for unilateral sensorineural loss: MRI with gadolinium. Aminoglycosides for a conductive loss: they cause sensorineural loss. Drainage culture: it grows only the superinfecting organisms. Chronic suppurative otitis media for drainage through a perforation: a secondary acquired cholesteatoma can follow drum injury, so look for the mass.
Pairs with Part II Sinusitis and Its Complications applies the same logic to the neighboring air-filled space, where a chronic infection of a bony cavity is dangerous because of what it erodes into. Congenital Infections (TORCH) covers congenital cytomegalovirus, the commonest nonhereditary cause of childhood sensorineural loss.
Transferable rule

Sort the loss with the forks, then read the drum: is it intact, and is the mass on it or in the canal? When the options describe processes rather than diseases, translate the diagnosis into its mechanism first; discharge that fails adequate antibiotics is a symptom of something structural.
